title: The Missionaries of Charity (1950)
hook: the sisters in white and blue saris, begun by Teresa of Calcutta, who care for the dying

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four churchwomen, among them Jean Donovan, who were asked to come home and didn't. Your line was they stayed with the poor. Who did you stay a little longer with? Today, sisters whose whole work is staying. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

A long room in Kolkata, beside a Hindu temple. Rows of low beds. On each, someone who was found on the street, too sick to walk. A sister in a white sari with blue stripes kneels at one of them with a basin of water. She is washing a man's feet. He may not live through the week, and she knows it. She is not there to cure him. She is there so that he does not die alone, unwashed, unnamed. The house is called Nirmal Hriday. The sisters are the Missionaries of Charity.
screen: `A LONG ROOM IN KOLKATA.` → `A SISTER WITH A BASIN.` → `SO NO ONE DIES ALONE.`

segments.voice: The order was begun by the woman Catholics now call Saint Teresa of Calcutta, Mother Teresa, a teacher who left her convent school to live among the poorest people of the city. Four things to know. First, the promise. Like other sisters, they make vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. Their rule adds one more promise: wholehearted and free service to the poorest of the poor. Free means no payment, ever. Second, the thirst. In their chapels, beside the crucifix, the sisters put two words from the cross in John's Gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "I thirst." The sisters hear in them Jesus thirsting for love, and they see him in the person on the bed. Third, the work, spread wide. The order grew far beyond Kolkata: homes for the dying, for abandoned children, for people with leprosy, for people with AIDS, soup kitchens in big Western cities. There are brothers and priests in the same family now too. The work is plain: washing, feeding, sitting, holding a hand. Fourth, the questions. Not everyone has praised it. Some critics, including doctors who visited, questioned the standard of medical care in the homes. Supporters answer that the homes were meant for comfort and presence at the end, not for hospital treatment. Both are part of the honest story. Today's line comes from a British journalist who filmed the sisters. He called his book Something Beautiful for God, after a phrase tradition links with Mother Teresa. Not something impressive. Something beautiful, like a clean bed and a held hand.
screen: `A TEACHER LEAVES HER SCHOOL.` · `FREE SERVICE TO THE POOREST.` · `I THIRST, BESIDE THE CROSS.` · `PRAISED, AND QUESTIONED.` · then, large: `I THIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who is dying, or very ill, in mind. Settle, and breathe. It might be a grandparent, a friend in a hospice, a neighbor you haven't seen in months, or a stranger in a hospital you passed. Picture their room. Picture someone sitting with them. Then ask, gently, whether that someone could be you: a visit, a phone call, a card, an hour of sitting. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the people who care for the dying. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Nirmal Hriday. The house in Kolkata where the Missionaries of Charity cared for the dying, so that no one died alone, unwashed or unnamed.
Your line: something beautiful. Today, if you can, make that visit or that call. If you can't, do one plain, unseen kindness for someone who can't repay it. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Missionaries of Charity sisters, in their white saris with blue borders, run homes for the dying, the abandoned and the sick in many countries, and volunteers of any faith or none can often come to help with the daily washing, feeding and cleaning.
